---

## Exam Syllabus

### English
Grammar: Tenses, articles, prepositions, conjunctions, voice (active/passive), narration (direct/indirect), sentence completion, error correction.
Vocabulary: Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases.
Comprehension: Reading passages with 5 to 10 questions per passage.

Most candidates score 60 to 80 out of 100 in English. It's manageable with 30 to 45 days of dedicated practice on previous CDS English papers.

### General Knowledge
- Current events (national and international), last 6 to 8 months
- Indian history, especially Freedom Struggle (1857 to 1947) and Constitution
- Indian geography and world geography
- General science, Physics, Chemistry, Biology (Class 10 NCERT level)
- Defence news and Indian military history

NCERT Class 9 to 10 textbooks are the GK backbone. For current affairs, use any standard monthly booklet.

### Elementary Mathematics (IMA/INA/AFA only)
- Arithmetic: Percentage, ratio, profit-loss, simple and compound interest, time-work, time-distance
- Algebra: Linear equations, quadratic equations, logarithms
- Geometry: Triangle theorems, circle properties, parallel lines
- Mensuration: Areas and volumes of standard shapes
- Statistics: Mean, median, mode, basic frequency distribution

CDS Maths is Class 10 level, not JEE, not even NDA level. But the negative marking means you must be accurate, not just fast.

---

## The SSB Interview: Equal to Written Marks

The SSB carries the same marks as the written exam. For IMA/INA/AFA, 300 marks written + 300 marks SSB = 600 total. For OTA, 200 + 200 = 400 total.

The SSB process unfolds over 5 days at SSB centres across India (Allahabad, Bhopal, Bangalore, Mysore, Kapurthala, Coimbatore, and others assigned based on your chosen academy):

**Day 1: Screening:**
- Officer Intelligence Rating (OIR) test, verbal and non-verbal reasoning
- Picture Perception and Discussion Test (PPDT), you describe a picture, write a story, and discuss it in a group

About 30 to 40% of candidates are screened in after Day 1. The rest are sent back the same day.

**Days 2 to 4: Psychological and Group Testing (for those who clear screening):**
- **TAT (Thematic Apperception Test):** You see 11 pictures + 1 blank slide, write a story for each in 4 minutes
- **WAT (Word Association Test):** 60 words flashed at 15 seconds each: write the first sentence that comes to mind
- **SRT (Situation Reaction Test):** 60 situations in 30 minutes: how do you respond?
- **SD (Self Description):** What does your family/friends/teachers say about you? What do you think of yourself?
- **Group Discussions:** 5 to 10 candidates, 2 rounds, defence and civilian topics
- **Group Planning Exercise:** Group solves a situation on a map
- **Progressive Group Task / Half Group Task:** Outdoor problem-solving activities with obstacles
- **Command Task:** You command your group to complete a task
- **Lecturette:** 3-minute talk on a chosen topic

**Day 5: Conference:**
All SSB officers discuss each candidate collectively. Final recommendation.

---

## Salary and Career After Commissioning

After completing training and commissioning:

| Rank | Pay Level | Basic Pay | MSP | Approximate Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lieutenant (Army) | Level 10 | ₹56,100 | ₹15,500 | ~₹80,000 to 1,00,000/month |
| Sub-Lieutenant (Navy) | Level 10 | ₹56,100 | ₹15,500 | ~₹80,000 to 1,00,000/month |
| Flying Officer (Air Force) | Level 10 | ₹56,100 | ₹15,500 | ~₹80,000 to 1,00,000/month |

In addition to salary: free accommodation, food allowance, medical benefits for family, Canteen Stores Department (CSD) facilities, and Group Insurance.

**IMA/INA/AFA → Permanent Commission:** Long-term career up to Colonel/Commodore/Group Captain or higher based on merit.

**OTA → Short Service Commission:** Initial 10 + 4 years (extendable). Option to apply for Permanent Commission after 5 years based on vacancies and performance. Many SSC officers transition to civil service or defence PSUs after service.

---

## What happens now the exam is over

**Days 1 to 30: Foundation**
- English: Solve previous 5 years' CDS English papers. Note every grammar rule you missed. Use Wren & Martin for grammar reference.
- GK: Read NCERT Class 9 to 10 History, Geography, Science. Make short notes on each chapter.
- Maths (if applying for IMA/INA/AFA): Revise Class 9 to 10 NCERT Maths thoroughly. Solve R.S. Aggarwal or similar for practice.

**Days 31 to 60: Practice and Mock Tests**
- Solve 2 to 3 full CDS mock tests per week under timed conditions (2 hours per paper)
- Current affairs: Read monthly current affairs booklet for April, September 2026
- Focus on accuracy, CDS negative marking punishes random guessing

**Days 61 to 94: Revision and Accuracy Drills**
- Revise weak chapters identified from mock tests
- Focus on eliminating avoidable errors in English grammar and Maths calculations
- Physical fitness: Start running and basic fitness training if you haven't, SSB involves outdoor physical tasks

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: I'm a Commerce graduate. Can I apply for IMA?**
Yes. IMA requires any graduation, BA, BCom, BSc, B.Tech, LLB are all eligible. The CDS written exam tests English, GK, and Elementary Maths, none of which require a specific academic stream.

**Q: I want to be a pilot. Is CDS the right path?**
For Air Force pilots: AFA through CDS is one path. AFCAT (Air Force Common Admission Test) is another. Both lead to the Air Force Academy. Check AFCAT if you don't meet CDS age requirements or want a direct Air Force-specific route.

**Q: Can I apply for both IMA and OTA in the same application?**
No. You apply for specific academy/course choices in your preference order. You can indicate multiple preferences within one application, but your exam papers depend on which academies you've opted for (if OTA only = 2 papers; if IMA/INA/AFA = 3 papers).

**Q: What is the difference between Permanent Commission and Short Service Commission?**
Permanent Commission (IMA/INA/AFA) offers a full military career until retirement age (typically 54 to 60 years depending on rank). Short Service Commission (OTA) is a contractual term of service, 10 years initially, extendable by 4 more years (total 14 years). After 14 years you exit, or apply for PC conversion. Both are commissioned officer roles, the difference is career length.

**Q: I failed SSB once. Can I apply again?**
Yes. There is no restriction on the number of CDS/SSB attempts, as long as you meet the age and qualification criteria at the time of application.

---

## Official Links

- UPSC Official Site: [upsc.gov.in](https://upsc.gov.in)
- Apply Online (when open): [upsconline.nic.in](https://upsconline.nic.in)

---

changes.content:
## UPSC Civil Services 2026: Mains starts 21 August

UPSC Civil Services Examination 2026 is recruiting for 933 posts across the Group A and Group B services. The Main examination ran on 21, 22, 23, 29 and 30 August 2026 and is over. Candidates who sat it are waiting on the result, which across the last five cycles has come 60 to 75 days after the final paper, putting it around late October to mid-November on that pattern rather than on any announced date.

The cycle so far: UPSC notified the examination on 4 February 2026, applications ran to 27 February, the Preliminary examination was held on 24 May 2026, and the Prelims result was declared on 15 June 2026. The Detailed Application Form I window ran from 19 to 28 June 2026. What remains is the Mains, then the Personality Test.

One thing worth fixing at the outset, because candidates lose marks to it every year. Two of the nine Mains papers do not count towards your rank at all, and two more decide almost everything. Getting that allocation wrong in the final fortnight is expensive, so the paper structure section below is the part of this page to read first.

## The Mains schedule, day by day

The Main examination runs across five days, with two sessions on each day.

| Date | Day |
|---|---|
| 21 August 2026 | Friday |
| 22 August 2026 | Saturday |
| 23 August 2026 | Sunday |
| 29 August 2026 | Friday |
| 30 August 2026 | Saturday |

Session timings are 9:00 am to 12:00 noon for the forenoon paper and 2:30 pm to 5:30 pm for the afternoon paper. Each paper is three hours.

Note the gap. The examination breaks after 23 August and resumes on 29 August, giving five clear days in between. That window usually falls before the optional subject papers, and how you use it matters: candidates who treat it as recovery time and candidates who treat it as revision time end up with noticeably different optional scores.

## Mains paper structure, and what actually counts

This is the table to internalise.

| Paper | Subject | Marks | Counts towards merit? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paper A | Indian language | 300 | No, qualifying only |
| Paper B | English | 300 | No, qualifying only |
| Paper I | Essay | 250 | Yes |
| Paper II | General Studies I | 250 | Yes |
| Paper III | General Studies II | 250 | Yes |
| Paper IV | General Studies III | 250 | Yes |
| Paper V | General Studies IV | 250 | Yes |
| Paper VI | Optional Subject Paper I | 250 | Yes |
| Paper VII | Optional Subject Paper II | 250 | Yes |

Seven papers at 250 marks each gives 1,750 marks that count. The Personality Test adds 275. Final merit is therefore out of **2,025 marks**.

Papers A and B carry 600 marks between them and contribute nothing to your rank. They are pass or fail. The qualifying standard is modest, typically set around 25 per cent, but the consequence of failing is absolute: if you do not clear Paper A or Paper B, UPSC does not evaluate your other seven papers at all. A candidate can write an excellent Essay, four strong General Studies papers and two good optional papers, and have none of them read.

Candidates from English-medium backgrounds underestimate Paper A, the Indian language paper. Candidates educated in regional-medium schools sometimes underestimate Paper B. Both mistakes end the attempt in exactly the same way, and both are avoidable with a few hours of practice on the prescribed formats: comprehension, précis, translation, and short composition.

## Where the marks are actually decided

Of the 1,750 counted marks, the optional subject carries 500 across two papers. That is more than any single General Studies paper and more than the Essay. It is also the most controllable component, because it is a defined syllabus you have studied for months rather than an open-ended current affairs canvas.

The four General Studies papers carry 1,000 marks combined. General Studies IV, the ethics paper, is the one candidates most often underprepare and the one where marks move most for modest effort, because a structured approach to case studies produces visible gains.

The Essay at 250 marks is a single paper with two essays of 125 marks each. It rewards structure and breadth of illustration rather than specialised knowledge, and it is frequently the difference between a rank and a near miss.

## Prelims pattern, for the next cycle

If you are targeting CSE 2027, the Preliminary examination is where the funnel narrows hardest.

| Paper | Content | Questions | Marks | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Paper I | General Studies | 100 | 200 | Decides who reaches Mains |
| Paper II | CSAT (aptitude) | 80 | 200 | Qualifying at 33 per cent |

Both papers are objective with negative marking, and both are two hours. Paper II being qualifying at 33 per cent means you need 66.7 marks out of 200 to pass it, and marks above that add nothing. Paper I alone decides the Prelims cutoff.

Prelims marks do not carry into the Mains or the final merit. They exist only to shortlist. That is worth remembering, because candidates sometimes treat a high Prelims score as a head start, and it is not one.

## Vacancies

CSE 2026 carries 933 vacancies, including 33 reserved for Persons with Benchmark Disabilities. These are distributed across the services, and the service-wise split is finalised later in the cycle rather than announced with the notification.

The services filled through this examination include the Indian Administrative Service, the Indian Police Service, the Indian Foreign Service, the Indian Revenue Service in both Income Tax and Customs and Indirect Taxes, the Indian Audit and Accounts Service, the Indian Railway Management Service, the Indian Defence Accounts Service, the Indian Information Service, and several other Group A and Group B services including the DANICS and DANIPS cadres.

Service allocation depends on your final rank and the preferences you submit in the Detailed Application Form, along with category and cadre rules. The top ranks generally clear IAS and IFS; the range of services accessible widens considerably as you move down the list.

## Eligibility

On age, candidates must be between 21 and 32 years as on 1 August 2026, with relaxation of 3 years for OBC candidates, 5 years for SC and ST candidates, and further relaxation for defence service personnel, ex-servicemen and PwBD candidates as specified.

On attempts, general category candidates get 6 attempts, OBC candidates get 9, and SC and ST candidates have no numerical limit but remain bound by the upper age limit. PwBD candidates get 9 attempts in the general and OBC categories. An attempt counts when you appear in at least one paper of the Preliminary examination.

On education, a bachelor's degree from a recognised university is required. Final-year students may apply for the Preliminary examination but must produce proof of passing before the Mains.

The application fee is Rs 100 for general, OBC and EWS male candidates. Female candidates and SC, ST and PwBD candidates pay nothing.

## Salary and what the job pays

An officer entering through this examination begins at Level 10 of the pay matrix with a basic pay of Rs 56,100 a month, plus dearness allowance, house rent allowance by city class, and transport allowance. Gross monthly pay at entry commonly works out well above the basic figure.

Progression runs through defined stages: Junior Time Scale at Level 10, Senior Time Scale at Level 11, Junior Administrative Grade at Level 12, Selection Grade at Level 13, Super Time Scale at Level 14, and upward to Level 15, 16, 17 and finally Level 18 for a Cabinet Secretary at Rs 2,50,000.

The non-cash side is substantial and frequently understated in comparisons: official accommodation, official vehicle and staff at appropriate levels, medical facilities, security of tenure, and pension benefits under the applicable rules. The counterweight is genuine and worth stating too: postings are transferable, early district assignments can be remote, and the working hours in field postings are long.

## Preparing in the final fortnight

With the Mains 17 days out, the useful moves are narrow and specific.

Stop consuming new material. Two weeks before a descriptive examination, the marginal value of a new source is near zero and the cost in revision time is real. Work from notes you already have.

Write full-length papers under the clock. Three hours, 20 questions, by hand. Mains is as much an endurance and time-allocation problem as a knowledge one, and candidates who have not written a full paper in weeks discover on day one that their hand tires and their last five answers suffer.

Settle on a template you can apply to any dilemma: identify the stakeholders, name the competing values, set out the options with their consequences, then commit to a decision and justify it. General Studies II covers the Constitution, polity, governance, social justice and international relations: the structure and functioning of the executive, legislature and judiciary, devolution of powers, statutory and constitutional bodies, government policies and interventions, welfare schemes, and India's relations with its neighbourhood and the wider world.

General Studies III covers the economy, agriculture, science and technology, environment, internal security and disaster management: growth and development, budgeting, cropping patterns, food processing, land reforms, infrastructure, technology missions, biodiversity, and security challenges including cyber security and money laundering.

## TNPSC Group 2 and 2A 2026: the dates and the distinction

TNPSC Group 2 and 2A is the Combined Civil Services Examination II, run by the Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission, and it fills clerical and supervisory posts across the state government. For the 2026 cycle, TNPSC released the notification on 11 August 2026 and the preliminary examination is scheduled for 1 November 2026.

Before the dates, the distinction, because it decides how you prepare. Group 2 and Group 2A are advertised together, use the same preliminary examination, and then diverge completely at the mains stage. Group 2 posts have a descriptive mains paper and an interview. Group 2A posts have an objective mains paper and no interview.

Candidates routinely apply to both, clear the same prelims, and then discover in the mains hall that they have prepared for the wrong format. Writing a 300-mark descriptive General Studies paper and answering a 300-mark objective one are different skills, and the gap between knowing a fact and being able to write about it under time pressure is where the Group 2 mains separates candidates.

## Important dates

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Notification expected | 11 August 2026 |
| Preliminary examination (CCSE-II) | 1 November 2026 |
| Mains examination | To be announced after the prelims result |

The previous cycle gives a sense of the rhythm. It was notified on 15 July 2025 for 659 vacancies, its mains was revised to 15 March 2026, and the mains result has been declared. So the gap from notification to prelims runs a few months, and from prelims to mains several more, which makes this a year-long process rather than a quick one.

Because the 2026 notification is not out at the time of writing, the vacancy count for this cycle is not known. Treat 659 as an indication of scale from the previous cycle rather than a figure for 2026.

## What Group 2 and Group 2A posts actually are

Both groups sit in the same broad band of state government service, but the roles differ in character.

Group 2, the interview posts, are supervisory and field-facing roles. They include Deputy Commercial Tax Officer, Sub Registrar Grade II, Probation Officer, Senior Inspector of Cooperative Societies, Municipal Commissioner Grade II, and Assistant Inspector of Labour. These carry public dealing, inspection powers, and decision-making responsibility, which is why the commission attaches an interview.

Group 2A, the non-interview posts, are largely office and secretariat roles, including Assistant Section Officer in the Secretariat and assistant posts across departments and the Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission itself. The work is file-based rather than field-based.

The exact post list is set in each notification, so check the advertisement for the cycle you are applying to rather than assuming last year's list carries over.

## Preliminary examination pattern

One paper, common to both groups.

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Total questions | 200 |
| Total marks | 300 |
| Duration | 3 hours |
| Negative marking | None |
| Minimum qualifying | 90 marks out of 300 |
| Composition | 100 questions General Tamil or General English, 100 questions General Studies and Aptitude |

Two features shape strategy here. There is no negative marking, so every one of the 200 questions should carry an answer. And the prelims is purely a screening stage: your prelims marks do not carry into the final merit list. Clearing it at a comfortable margin is all that is required, and marks beyond that buy nothing.

The 90 out of 300 qualifying figure is the floor, not the real bar. The actual cutoff for being called to the mains is set by the number of vacancies and the number of candidates, and it sits well above the qualifying minimum in most cycles.

## Mains examination: two different exams

This is where the groups separate.

| | Group 2 (interview posts) | Group 2A (non-interview posts) |
|---|---|---|
| Paper I | Tamil eligibility test, SSLC standard, descriptive, 100 marks | Tamil eligibility test, SSLC standard, descriptive, 100 marks |
| Paper I role | Qualifying only | Qualifying only |
| Paper II | General Studies, degree standard, DESCRIPTIVE, 300 marks | General Studies with reasoning and language, OBJECTIVE, 300 marks |
| Interview | Yes | No |
| Merit built from | Paper II and interview | Paper II alone |

Paper I is a mandatory Tamil eligibility paper at SSLC standard, and it is qualifying. Its 100 marks do not enter your merit position. A candidate who writes a strong Paper I and a weak Paper II gains nothing from the former.

## CAT 2026: registration is open now

CAT 2026, the Common Admission Test for the IIMs and several hundred other business schools, is conducted this year by IIM Indore. Registration opened at 10:00 am on 3 August 2026 and closes at 5:00 pm on 22 September 2026, extended by a week from the original 15 September. The examination is on Sunday, 29 November 2026, in three slots across roughly 170 cities and more than 300 test centres.

If you intend to sit CAT this year, the window is open right now and it does not reopen. IIM Indore released the notification and information bulletin on 26 July 2026 on iimcat.ac.in.

Two things about CAT catch first-time candidates out, and both are structural rather than about difficulty. The sections are time-locked, so you cannot return to a section once its 40 minutes are gone. And a meaningful share of questions carry no negative marking at all, which changes how you should attempt them.

## Important dates

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Notification and information bulletin | 26 July 2026 |
| Registration opens | 3 August 2026, 10:00 am |
| Registration closes | 22 September 2026, 5:00 pm (extended from 15 September) |
| Admit card download | 4 November to 29 November 2026 |
| Examination | 29 November 2026, three slots |
| Result | Expected first week of January 2027 |

The gap between the close of registration and the examination is about ten weeks, which is the realistic preparation window for anyone starting now.

## Exam pattern

CAT is a computer based test of 68 questions over 120 minutes.

| Section | Questions | MCQ | TITA | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension (VARC) | 24 | 20 | 4 | 40 minutes |
| Data Interpretation and Logical Reasoning (DILR) | 22 | 11 | 11 | 40 minutes |
